sections.html:
The City's Department of Records is the recorder of deeds for Philadelphia County. It sits in City Hall, and the main line is (215) 686-2262. One office takes deeds, mortgages and other real estate documents for every neighborhood, because the city and county share the same borders.

Individuals file by mail or at the counter. Counter service needs an appointment, booked by email to appointments.records@phila.gov, and recording hours are weekdays from 8 a.m. until 3:30 p.m. Mailed documents go to City Hall, Room 111, 1400 John F. Kennedy Blvd., Philadelphia, PA 19107, along with a stamped, self-addressed envelope so the original can come back. Anyone dropping off three or more documents leaves them to be picked up later.

Title companies and businesses usually record electronically through Simplifile, CSC eRecording or ePN, and those filings are paid by ACH.

sections.h2: What a deed needs before it is accepted
sections.html:
Documents that miss the office's formatting and content rules are rejected, so a title company or lawyer normally prepares the deed. The Department advises against drafting one yourself and recommends title insurance.

  • White 8.5 by 11 inch paper, typed in 10 point black ink, one side only.
  • A 3 inch top margin on page one with the "Prepared by" and "Return to" details at the left, and 1 inch margins elsewhere.
  • A date, the typed names of every party, and signatures and a notary acknowledgment that match those names.
  • For a Philadelphia property, a metes and bounds description and the street address.
  • A signed, certified grantee address on deeds, mortgages and assignments.
  • The full consideration, with numbers that match the written amount.
  • The Philadelphia Real Estate Transfer Tax Certificate in duplicate and the Pennsylvania Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value, plus the tax unless the transfer is exempt.

A standard deed costs $278.75 on the current schedule, and a few special cases carry lower fees. These are the charges homeowners run into most.

DocumentFee
Deed$278.75

Payment can be cash, a money order, a business or certified check, or Visa, Mastercard, Discover or American Express. Cards add a 3.5 percent convenience fee, and personal checks are refused. Taxes and fees need separate checks: the state tax payable to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, and the City tax and recording fees payable to the City of Philadelphia. A surviving spouse named on the deed can have part of the fee waived, and military discharge papers are recorded and copied free.

The total rate is 4.578 percent of the sale price: 3.578 percent for the City plus 1 percent for the Commonwealth. The City portion rose from 3.278 percent on July 1, 2025, and the City says the increase pays for affordable housing programs.

The tax is owed when the deed is presented for recording, and the City allows up to 30 days to pay after the property is acquired. Buyer and seller usually divide it at closing, yet the City can collect the whole amount from either one, so buyers want it paid at settlement. Misstating the transaction or never recording it can bring a penalty of up to 50 percent of the tax.

When no price exists, as with a gift or foreclosure, the tax runs on a computed value: the assessed value times the state's Common Level Ratio, then times the rate. Most transfers among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are exempt, with documents required for each claim.

sections.h2: Do inherited or estate-sold homes pay transfer tax?
sections.html:
It depends on how title moves. A transfer under a will can be exempt, but tax is due if mortgages, liens or debts on the home are still unpaid at the time of transfer. A home bought from an estate is not exempt. If a will leaves a property to several heirs and one buys out the others, tax is owed on that purchase.

  • Heirs who keep the property usually record a deed from the estate and show the family relationship.
  • Heirs who sell record the deed to the buyer, and that sale carries the full transfer tax.
  • If title is still in a deceased owner's name, ask the title company which estate papers it needs before it will insure the sale.

sections.h2: How to pay the transfer tax
sections.html:
There are three ways to pay, and the title company usually picks the first or second.

  • Online through the Philadelphia Tax Center, by logging in or using the Letter ID printed at the top of the bill.
  • In person, when the deed is filed with the Department of Records.
  • By mail, with two copies of the City certificate, one copy of the state Statement of Value form, and three certified checks: one for the recording fee, one for the City tax and one for the Commonwealth tax.

The tax reaches more than sales. Deeds, leases of 30 years or longer, easements, life estates, entity transfers and transfers of 75 percent or more of a real estate company all trigger it.

The Department also runs the City Archives. Copies of deeds from 1683 to 1955 cost $2 a page, mortgages from 1748 to 1963 are also $2 a page, and a search of deeds, mortgages and other land records is $20 an hour with a $20 minimum. A plot plan copy is $10, and a certified copy is $2 per document. These records come in handy when an old gap in ownership needs tracing before a sale.

sections.h2: Where recording fits in a Philadelphia sale
sections.html:
Recording comes last in the closing sequence, and the title company usually files it. The seller signs the deed, the title company or buyer assembles the transfer tax certificates, pays the tax and fee, and files the package with the Department of Records.

Ahead of that, the title search looks at property tax, water and sewer balances, since each can sit as a lien. A seller with tax or lien problems can still close if the payoff is arranged in advance. A cash buyer working through a title company can handle the transfer tax split and the recording as part of one closing.

Most of the work lands on the title company, but a seller can save time by doing a few things early.

  1. Confirm who will file: the title company by electronic recording, or you by mail or with an appointment at City Hall.
  2. If you are filing by mail, prepare the stamped, self-addressed envelope for the original and send the package to Room 111.
  3. Ask the title company how the transfer tax will be split and whether any exemption applies.
  4. Make sure checks are separate: the Commonwealth tax on one, and the City tax and recording fees on another. Personal checks are refused.
  5. Clear up any tax, water or sewer balance before the closing date, or have the payoff arranged in advance.

faqs.q: Which office files my Philadelphia deed?
faqs.a: The Department of Records in City Hall, Room 111, either by mail or in person with an appointment. Businesses can also record electronically through a third party vendor.

faqs.q: What fee applies to a standard Philadelphia deed?
faqs.a: The deed fee is $278.75, plus the realty transfer tax unless the transfer is exempt. A deed for a deceased spouse or partner is $43.75. Check the current fee schedule before you send payment.

faqs.q: What is the realty transfer tax rate in Philadelphia?
faqs.a: It is 4.578 percent, made up of 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the state. It falls due at recording, and the City allows up to 30 days to pay.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed without a lawyer?
faqs.a: It is possible, but the Department advises against preparing a deed yourself. Use a lawyer, title company or other professional, and consider title insurance.

faqs.q: Does the Department of Records take personal checks?
faqs.a: No. It accepts cash, money orders, business or certified checks, and cards with a 3.5 percent fee. Taxes and fees go on separate checks.
